Title: Why draw when you can Withdraw?

Messages.Author: hamdamcwa
Messages.Body:
This is something that I have been thinking about for a while. The
Withdraw option is far more appealing that a draw or a time out. Sure,
there are more conditions to a Withdraw in theory, but in any given
game they can usually be reached without too much bother.

e.g. 5 minutes to the end of a game. 3 methusulas left. The game is
virtually a stalemate, each player has roughly the same amount of pool
(above 10). There are no "table shagging" effects in play (Anarch
Revolt, Smiling jack, etc) and no-one is likely to oust. Each player
has about 25 cards in their library. The options are:

1) Keep going and get timed out - 0.5 VP each

2) Call it a draw - 0.5VP each

3) Manufacture a withdraw to get 1VP each.

How do you manufacture a Withdraw? Simple. Everyone's takes the next
26 goes in the space of 5 mins. Everyone's only action in their turn
is to discard a card or more if they have the capacity. Once
everyone's library is empty, withdraw. This is almost like a table
splitting deal, but at the other end of the scale (i.e. maximising VPs
by arranging NOT to play!). In fact, I doubt if most judges wouldn't
even enforce the "letter of the law" regarding the conditions of
withdrawing if it is the clear intent of all the players in the game -
again much like a Draw.

In fact, since the Withdraw option is availible, surely every game
that heads down the stalemate route MUST (by virtue of the rules) try
to engage a mutual withdraw to gain more VPs than a stalemate? Sure,
there are situations where this isn't quite so easy (Anarch Revolts
being a key one, but I'm talking about games where there are lots of
static or relevant table effects in play), but in the vast majority of
games, these can be circumvented in a turn or two when the game has
reached an impasse.

So here's the question - why is the "we'll accept a draw" option still
around? Why can't the Draw option be replaced permenantly with a
withdraw (either actual or "virtual" - i.e. lots of cards left but all
players are willing)?
Are there any situations where a Draw seriously is the only way of
stopping the game other than a time out?

Thoughts people?

Dave
Watford

Performing no non-mandatory activity in your (or anyone else's) turn
except discarding is an example of playing the game. It is not an
example of NOT playing.

> even enforce the "letter of the law" regarding the conditions of
> withdrawing if it is the clear intent of all the players in the game -
> again much like a Draw.

I would be very surprised to find judges not enforcing rules that they
know. I would be very interested to hear of cases where a judge allows
known rules violations.

> In fact, since the Withdraw option is availible, surely every game
> that heads down the stalemate route MUST (by virtue of the rules) try
> to engage a mutual withdraw to gain more VPs than a stalemate?

No. You cannot force a player to trust another player to honor a deal.

Messages.Body:

> So here's the question - why is the "we'll accept a draw" option still

> withdraw (either actual or "virtual" - i.e. lots of cards left but all
> players are willing)?
> Are there any situations where a Draw seriously is the only way of
> stopping the game other than a time out?

Well, mostly I guess because the player's can't trust eachother. Not
that this is a bad thing, mind you. But you've just given your predator
26 turns to put together the perfect hand. Or maybe your predator is
able to oust you, but not without fear of being ousted by his predator.
His predator withdraws, and your predator decides that 2 VPs are
better than 1.

And, of course, there's also Brinksmanship. Might not be found in many
decks, but all it would take would be once to sour people on the idea of
a voluntary group withdrawal.

--Colin McGuigan

I have judged several events (also big ones) and in a given game when there
was :

a) enough time left
b) everyone agreeing on a withdrawal
c) everyone agreeing to stop the game immediately

I allowed the players to withdraw immediately without the ridiculous 5-10
min of card discarding.
Especially when there is little time between rounds and players are hungry
this was always a welcome decisicion.
It might have been against the rules, but sometimes I prefer common sense
instead of rules.

Messages.Author: Halcyan 2
Messages.Body:
>> In fact, since the Withdraw option is availible, surely every game
>> that heads down the stalemate route MUST (by virtue of the rules) try
>> to engage a mutual withdraw to gain more VPs than a stalemate?
>
>No. You cannot force a player to trust another player to honor a deal.

LSJ has really hit the nail on the head with this part.

There's really an important trust issue with attempts to withdrawals. For the
judges who simply allow a table withdrawal since everyone "agrees" to a
withdrawal, he might be foiling the plans of one of the players who plans to do
a 180 at the last minute.

Similarly, a player who has the advantage in permanents might very well want to
see the combat monster or intercept wall deck run out of cards this way.

Halcyan 2

>see the combat monster or intercept wall deck run out of cards this way.

I don't find the idea of someone breaking a mutual withdrawal plan realistic.
Since it takes so little time to accomplish, might as well wait til the last
few minutes. Since it takes a bunch of time to oust people you were thinking
of agreeing to withdraw with, you won't have time to oust once you enact your
withdrawal plan. If there's a big disparity in permanents, the plan is
unlikely to occur or likely to occur only so late as to make it impossible to
oust anyone. It's easy enough to see someone trying to back out of an
agreement, which leaves the game in basically the same situation if everyone
stops turbowithdrawing. If you can oust someone whether with the "perfect
hand" or not, there was never any basis for a withdrawal agreement in the first
place.

I think more credit should be given to players. The agree to a draw rule
serves no purpose. There's no benefit to playing out a mutual withdrawal.

It sounds like no one at the table can do anything to stop you from ousting
your prey whether there's a plan to withdraw in place or not. I don't see
anything sneaky or dealbreaky about this. Basically, the game turns out as
expected, though the other players may want to stop a TW by no longer
attempting to withdraw. The plan to withdraw was poorly conceived in the first
place if someone had the time to oust anyone.

>It does happen

What happens every single time I see players agree to withdraw is that people
stop looking at what they draw and discard as fast as they possibly can in
order to make sure it gets done in time because it's required to go through the
motions. Kind of hard to be sneaky when you aren't aware of what you are
capable of doing.

If people are going to take the time to study their hands every time they
discard, then someone thinks ousting someone is possible and you might as well
keep playing until you don't have time to oust anyone before going into
turbowithdrawal mode.
